name: Cochlear nuclei
summary: The dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei drape over the inferior cerebellar peduncle at the pontomedullary junction and receive every fiber of the cochlear nerve. From them the auditory pathway becomes bilateral almost at once: second-order axons cross in the trapezoid body to the contralateral superior olive and lateral lemniscus, while others ascend on the same side. This early bilaterality is why a single central lesion above the nuclei never causes deafness in one ear, whereas a lesion of the nerve or nuclei does.

anatomy.location: Lateral surface of the inferior cerebellar peduncle at the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle, where the cochlear nerve enters at the cerebellopontine angle.

function: First central relay of hearing; begins frequency analysis and the separation of pathways for sound localization (ventral nucleus) and spectral analysis (dorsal nucleus).

bestView.label: lateral recess of the fourth ventricle at the cochlear nerve entry
cerebellopontine angle and internal acoustic meatus

imaging.normalAppearance: Not resolved on routine MRI; the cochlear nerve itself is seen on high-resolution T2 (CISS/FIESTA) entering the brainstem at the lateral recess. AICA infarcts that include the nuclei show lateral pontomedullary restriction.

pathology.finding: Lateral pontomedullary and anterior inferior cerebellar restricted diffusion with acute unilateral hearing loss.
Enhancing mass at the internal acoustic meatus and cerebellopontine angle compressing the nerve before it reaches the nuclei.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: High-resolution T2 of the internal acoustic meatus; DWI for infarct; audiometry

lesionEffects.mechanism: Nerve or cochlear nuclei, before the pathway becomes bilateral

lesionEffects.deficit: Bilateral mild hearing loss and poor localization from a higher lesion
lesionEffects.mechanism: Lesions above the nuclei affect both ears because of the crossing

examination: Whisper test and finger rub in each ear
Rinne and Weber tuning-fork tests to separate conductive from sensorineural loss
pearls: Unilateral deafness is a nerve, cochlear nucleus or cochlear problem, never a hemispheric one
Sudden deafness with vertigo and ataxia is an AICA stroke until proven otherwise
